notes: Batch C08-B2 covers C08-06, C08-24, C08-25, C08-18 and C08-26. Existing evidence files were checked first. Sherrington 2019 (C01-B2) and Hauer 2012 (C02-B3) were reused, and their PubMed abstracts were re-opened. Full texts read in PMC: GREAT (IJGP), the GREAT protocol, Crawley 2023, DAPA and WHELD. The HTA report and the Cochrane CST review returned only the abstract and plain-language summary. Scite reached its monthly limit, so corrections and retractions were checked in PubMed (retracted publication, expression of concern and published erratum searches); no notices were found. NICE NG97 could not be opened (WebFetch blocked; no copy in Drive). Its recommendations are recorded from a search extract and corroborated by peer-reviewed papers. Drive search results included confidential case files (HS25000051 series); these were not opened. New conflicting evidence was found for C08-25: the MIDDEL trial (2025) postdates the Cochrane search.

CR involved working collaboratively on up to three rehabilitation goals chosen by the participant, using a problem‐solving approach." ... "CR could potentially be delivered by therapists from various professional backgrounds; in this trial, the therapists were nine occupational therapists and one nurse." claims.qualifications: The methods list is the paper's general description of cognitive rehabilitation, not a record of what each participant used. On average therapists addressed two goals per person.

claims.claim: Participant-rated goal attainment improved with a large effect at 3 months (d 0.97) and was maintained at 9 months (d 0.94); carer ratings agreed (d 1.11 and 0.96). On the 0 to 10 goal scale, average ratings rose by 2.57 points with therapy and 0.86 points with usual treatment at 3 months.
claims.supporting_passage: IJGP abstract: "At 3 months, there were statistically significant large positive effects for participant-rated goal attainment (d = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.75-1.19), corroborated by informant ratings (d = 1.11; 95% CI, 0.89-1.34). These effects were maintained at 9 months for both participant (d = 0.94; 95% CI, 0.71-1.17) and informant (d = 0.96; 95% CI, 0.73-1.2) ratings." HTA abstract: "mean change in the CR arm: 2.57; mean change in the TAU arm: 0.86". IJGP full text, Methods: "The primary outcome was participant‐rated goal attainment at 3 months, recorded using a previously validated client‐centred attainment measure, a simple 0 to 10 scale that is accessible and feasible for people with cognitive impairment to complete; an improvement of 2 points in the goal attainment rating for any individual goal is considered to be clinically significant." ... "All participants chose up to three goals at baseline and rated current attainment; attainment ratings were then averaged across each participant's goals to give a single summary rating."
claims.location: IJGP abstract (Results) and Methods (Outcomes); HTA abstract (Results)
claims.pico_timeframe: P: GREAT participants. I: cognitive rehabilitation. C: usual treatment. O: self-rated (and carer-rated) attainment of each person's own goals, 0 to 10 scale averaged across goals. T: 3 and 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: People rated how well they were managing each of their own goals on a 0 to 10 scale. After 3 months, ratings rose by about 2.6 points on average with therapy, compared with about 0.9 points with usual care. The researchers called this a large effect, it was still there at 9 months, and family members' ratings agreed.
claims.qualifications: Ratings came from participants and family members, who knew whether therapy had been given; the researchers who collected the ratings were blind. The 2.57 vs 0.86 figures are average changes in the goal score, not the proportion of people who improved. A 2-point gain on a single goal is the trial's threshold for a clinically significant change.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Because the raters knew their allocation and the therapy worked directly on these goals, some of the gain may reflect expectation or attention; the authors say the design could not rule out non-specific effects of therapist contact (see C08-06-f).

carer-rated effect size at 3 months

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in quality of life, mood, self-efficacy or cognition (or in carer stress and quality of life).
claims.supporting_passage: IJGP abstract: "Secondary outcomes at 3 and 9 months included informant-reported goal attainment, quality of life, mood, self-efficacy, and cognition and study partner stress and quality of life." ... "There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes." Full text, Results: "Following Bonferroni correction, there were no significant differences. Effect sizes were small to negligible, although in some cases with wide confidence intervals."
claims.pico_timeframe: Same trial; standard scales of quality of life, mood, self-efficacy, cognition and carer outcomes at 3 and 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: On the standard questionnaires for quality of life, mood, confidence and memory and thinking, the trial did not show a clear difference between the groups.
claims.qualifications: 'No significant difference' after Bonferroni correction, with small to negligible effect sizes and some wide confidence intervals: not proof of no effect.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors say no change in cognitive scores was expected, because the therapy does not aim to improve cognition, and few participants had depression or anxiety at the start (C08-06-f). So the standard scales were not a fair test of what the therapy targets; the post should say this and not imply the scales 'failed'.

claims.claim: The gains related to the goals directly targeted in therapy; for the goals actually worked on, the improvement was larger (2.84 points at 3 months).
claims.supporting_passage: IJGP abstract: "The observed gains related to goals directly targeted in the therapy." Full text, Results: "The CR group participants identified 679 goals and worked on 481 (71%) of these with the therapists. Taking just the 481 goals that were addressed in therapy, the mean change in participants' goal attainment ratings was an improvement of 2.84 points (SD 2.84) at 3 months and 2.77 points (SD 3.18) at 9 months, while." Limitations: "While participants were invited to select up to three goals, on average, the therapists were able to address two goals per participant. The primary outcome was based on ratings of progress with all goals identified at baseline, rather than just those goals that were actually addressed; therefore, the overall estimate of improvement in goal attainment is a conservative one. Ratings for the goals that were directly addressed showed a clinically meaningful degree of change."
claims.location: IJGP abstract (Results); Results (goal attainment); Discussion (Strengths and limitations)
claims.pico_timeframe: Rehabilitation group only: 679 goals identified, 481 worked on; change from baseline at 3 and 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: The improvement was in the specific goals people worked on with the therapist. It did not spread to general measures.
claims.qualifications: The 2.84-point figure is a within-group change for goals addressed in therapy, with no control comparison; use the between-group result (C08-06-c) as the headline.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Reading cautiously: the trial was single-blind (only researchers blinded) and the authors say it could not separate the specific effect of rehabilitation from non-specific effects of therapist contact; they also say the standard scales were not expected to change and may have missed wider benefits.
claims.supporting_passage: Full text, Methods: "This was a multicentre, single‐blind pragmatic RCT comparing CR added to usual treatment (CR) with usual treatment alone (TAU). Outcomes were assessed 3 and 9 months post randomisation." ... "All assessments were conducted in participants' homes by trained researchers blind to group allocation." Limitations: "The trial design did not allow us to conclusively demonstrate that benefits were due to the specific effects of CR rather than nonspecific effects of contact with a therapist; however, the observed gains related specifically to improvements in functional ability for goals directly targeted in the therapy, and in the pilot trial, CR demonstrated benefits over an active control condition." Discussion: "The finding of no differences in cognitive test scores was unsurprising as the intervention does not directly seek to improve cognitive function. As only a small proportion of participants reported clinical levels of depression or anxiety at baseline, there was little scope for the intervention to demonstrate improvements in these domains." ... "However, the qualitative findings were at odds with the results from secondary outcome measures. The intervention may therefore have provided wider benefits that were not detected by available standardised measures."
claims.location: IJGP Methods (Design; Assessments); Discussion (Strengths and limitations; How the findings relate to other evidence)
claims.pico_timeframe: Same trial.
claims.safe_wording: Two cautions. The people rating the goals knew they had had therapy, and the trial could not rule out that some of the benefit came from having an attentive visitor. Also, the therapy was never aimed at memory scores, so no change there is not a failure. The goal ratings measured what the therapy set out to change.
claims.qualifications: 'Single-blind' here means the researchers collecting outcomes were blind; participants and carers were not. The authors' suggestion that the questionnaires missed wider benefits rests on qualitative interviews and is their interpretation.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors point to their earlier pilot trial, in which rehabilitation beat an active control condition, as partial reassurance about non-specific effects.

claims.claim: Measured by quality-adjusted life years, the standard economic yardstick, the trial found no evidence of cost-effectiveness; measured against the goals, rehabilitation was cost-effective at willingness-to-pay values of £2,500 or more per unit improvement.
claims.supporting_passage: HTA abstract: "In the cost-utility analyses, there was no evidence of cost-effectiveness in terms of gains in the quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) of the person with dementia (measured using the DEMentia Quality Of Life questionnaire utility score) or the QALYs of the carer (measured using the EuroQol-5 Dimensions, three-level version) from either cost perspective. In the cost-effectiveness analyses, by reference to the primary outcome of participant-rated goal attainment, CR was cost-effective from both the health and social care perspective and the societal perspective at willingness-to-pay values of £2500 and above for improvement in the goal attainment measure."
claims.pico_timeframe: Economic evaluation alongside GREAT, 9 months.
claims.safe_wording: The same pattern showed up in the costings. Judged by the usual economic measure (quality-adjusted life years), the therapy showed no evidence of value for money. Judged by the goals people chose, it did.
claims.qualifications: Cost-effectiveness against the goal measure depends on how much a service is willing to pay per point of goal improvement (£2,500 or more); there is no agreed threshold for that measure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; this is the trial's own analysis.

In the 25 studies, with 1893 participants, reporting the widely used MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination) test for cognitive function in dementia, there was moderate-quality evidence of a clinically important difference of 1.99 points between CS and controls (95% CI: 1.24, 2.74)." ... "we found moderate-quality evidence of a slight improvement in self-reported QoL (18 studies, 1584 participants; SMD: 0.25 [95% CI: 0.07, 0.42]) as well as in QoL ratings made by proxies (staff or caregivers). We found high-quality evidence for clinically relevant improvements in staff/interviewer ratings of communication and social interaction (5 studies, 702 participants; SMD: 0.53 [95% CI: 0.36, 0.70])" ... "We found moderate-quality evidence that overall CS made little or no difference to caregivers' mood or anxiety." ... "We found a high level of inconsistency between studies in relation to both cognitive outcomes and QoL." Plain-language summary: "This benefit equates roughly to a six‐month delay in the cognitive decline usually expected in mild‐to‐moderate dementia." claims.pico_timeframe: P: people with mild to moderate dementia, community and care homes. I: cognitive stimulation (mostly group). C: usual care or unstructured activity. claims.claim: At 12 months, ADAS-cog scores were slightly worse in the exercise group (adjusted difference 1.4 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 2.6, on a 0 to 70 scale where higher is worse); the programme did not slow cognitive decline, and the authors judged the difference small with uncertain clinical relevance.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "By 12 months the mean ADAS-cog score had increased to 25.2 (SD 12.3) in the exercise arm and 23.8 (SD 10.4) in the usual care arm (adjusted between group difference -1.4, 95% confidence interval -2.6 to -0.2, P=0.03). This indicates greater cognitive impairment in the exercise group, although the average difference is small and clinical relevance uncertain." ... "A moderate to high intensity aerobic and strength exercise training programme does not slow cognitive impairment in people with mild to moderate dementia." Full text, Outcomes: "(ADAS-cog 11 item scale, scored 0 to 70; higher scores indicate worse cognitive impairment)". Interpretation: "We did not prespecify a value for a negative effect, but the average effect observed was smaller than our prespecified superiority target of 2.45 ADAS-cog points. An influential international consensus group suggests that a between group difference of 2 points (or 25%) might be worthwhile depending on the cost and safety profile of the intervention." ... "the treatment difference was at least half as much as the annual rate of decline." Conclusion: "does not slow cognitive decline and might worsen cognitive impairment in people with mild to moderate dementia."

claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Several smaller earlier trials reported cognitive benefit; the authors attribute this to weaker methods. Result applies to this moderate to high intensity programme.

Low to very low certainty evidence showed that they did not improve emotional well-being (SMD 0.14, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.56; 4 studies, 154 participants), anxiety (SMD -0.15, 95% CI -0.39 to 0.09; 7 studies, 282 participants), social behaviour (SMD 0.22, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.57; 2 studies; 121 participants) or cognition (SMD 0.19, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.41; 7 studies, 353 participants)."

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported from the GREAT HTA abstract and the IJGP full text. The numbers check out: 475 randomised; d 0.97 at 3 months and 0.94 at 9 months, participant-rated; carer ratings 1.11 and 0.96; no significant differences in quality of life, mood, self-efficacy or cognition; gains confined to the targeted goals. The judge's caution is confirmed and must be in the post. Ratings came from participants and carers who knew their allocation (single-blind: only the researchers were blinded). The authors say non-specific therapist contact could not be excluded, and that cognition and mood were not expected to change. So the post must not imply that the standard scales 'failed'. It should say they measured things the therapy did not target. A strong extra point for 'What gets counted': judged by QALYs the therapy showed no value for money, while judged by the goals it was cost-effective (C08-06-g). The sources do not report which goals participants chose (C08-06-h, not found), so do not name goal types. Describe the goals as everyday activities, and the methods as prompts, memory aids and practising the skill. Use 'about 2.6 vs 0.9 points on a 0 to 10 scale' rather than Cohen's d for the public.

Essential claims are supported. NICE recommends offering group CST in mild to moderate dementia: NG97 1.4.2 is a search extract only, but two peer-reviewed papers corroborate it. The format is 14 sessions over 7 weeks, usually about 45 minutes twice weekly in small groups. Spector 2003 (201 people) improved cognition and quality of life compared with controls. The Cochrane 2023 review (37 trials, 2,766 people) found a small short-term cognitive benefit: about 2 MMSE points, which the reviewers equate to roughly a six-month delay in decline, moderate quality. It also found clinically relevant gains in communication and social interaction (high quality), but only slight and inconsistent gains in quality of life. Three wording changes are required. (1) Drop 'often available through memory services or charities' and any statement that availability varies by area: no source was found (C08-18-e). Keep the practical question 'ask whether a group runs near you'. (2) Qualify quality of life as a slight benefit. (3) Present the benefit as short-term and small. Do not call CST the 'only' non-drug treatment NICE recommends, and attribute the recommendation to NICE in England.

The trial facts are supported from DAPA full text: 494 randomised; no slowing of decline; ADAS-cog 1.4 points worse at 12 months (95% CI 0.2 to 2.6); no differences in daily activities, behaviour, quality of life, carer outcomes or falls; six-minute walk up 18.1 m in the exercise arm. Two parts of the candidate's wording are not supported. (1) 'Too small to notice' (core insight and visual) is not supported. The authors call the clinical relevance uncertain, note the difference was at least half the usual annual decline, and conclude the programme 'might worsen cognitive impairment'. The complier estimate was 2.0 points worse. (2) 'Largest UK trial' is not verified; the authors say only that it was substantially larger than earlier trials. In addition, fitness was measured only in the exercise arm, so the authors cannot conclude definitely that the programme improved fitness. Exercise-for-falls evidence does not transfer to dementia: Sherrington 2019 excluded condition-specific trials, and DAPA found no falls difference. The positive close is supportable: Hauer 2012 shows dementia-adapted strength training improves strength and chair-standing.
candidates.revised_angle: A large trial in England (DAPA, 494 people with mild to moderate dementia) tested 4 months of fairly hard gym exercise. People got fitter and stronger during the classes. But a year later their memory and thinking had not declined more slowly. If anything, scores were slightly worse, by an amount whose importance is uncertain. Daily activities, behaviour, quality of life and falls did not differ. Position: offer exercise to people with dementia for strength, mobility and enjoyment (dementia-adapted strength training does build strength), without promising it will slow memory loss. The post should say this programme was moderate to high intensity, and should not claim falls prevention in dementia.

candidates.reason: The Cochrane 2025 figures and certainty levels are verified exactly: 30 studies, 1,720 people; at least 5 sessions; mostly group sessions in institutions. Against usual care, depressive symptoms 'probably improved slightly' (moderate certainty) and overall behaviour 'may have improved' (low certainty). Agitation or aggression were 'likely' not improved (moderate certainty), and no long-term effect was shown (low or very low certainty). Against other activities, music showed no clear advantage for mood. But the review's search ended in November 2023. The later MIDDEL trial (Lancet Healthy Longevity 2025; 1,021 care home residents with dementia and depressive symptoms, 86 units, 6 countries including the UK) found that neither group music therapy nor choir singing reduced depressive symptoms at 6 months. So the candidate's central positive claim, that music lifts mood a little, is now contested and cannot stand alone. The agitation point stands, and a Norwegian trial of daily personal playlists also found no change in agitation. The judge's point is confirmed: the evidence concerns structured sessions, mostly in care homes, not the radio.
candidates.revised_angle: Music and dementia: the trial evidence is weaker than the claims. The 2025 Cochrane review (30 trials of planned music sessions, mostly in care homes) found music probably does not calm agitation or aggression. It may lift low mood slightly while sessions continue, with no benefit shown a month after they stop. The largest trial since, in 1,021 care home residents in six countries, found that music therapy groups and choir singing did not ease depressive symptoms at 6 months. Position: offer music because the person enjoys it and it gives shared time with others, and judge it by whether they enjoy it. Do not use it as the treatment for agitation or low mood, or as a substitute for looking for the cause of distress. The 'enjoyment' point must be framed as a judgement, not a finding.

candidates.reason: Essential claims are supported from WHELD full text: 69 UK nursing homes; 847 randomised; 553 completed, with death the main reason for non-completion. Quality of life (d 0.24), agitation (0.23) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (0.30) improved by small amounts, most clearly in moderately severe dementia. Positive care interactions increased. Antipsychotic use (<10% at baseline) did not fall. The judge's concerns are confirmed and must shape the wording. Outcomes were proxy-rated by care staff. The authors describe the effects as 'marginal' clinically. The cost result is fragile: most of the £4,740 lower 9-month cost was accommodation charges (£4,399), and baseline costs already differed, so do not lead with 'cost less'. Say at most 'the researchers reported it did not add to overall costs', or omit it. The one component a home could start with (tailored social activity, about an hour a week per resident) can be offered as the authors' view and editorial judgement, because the trial tested the package as a whole.
